title: Fall Sesshin-Buddha, Occam, Danish Architects&British Grandmothers
speaker: Junka Ken Oates
summary: Junka Ken Oates tells how the Buddha's plain teaching of dissatisfaction, change, and interconnection grows into lists, among them the eighty-five Robert Thurman counts in his Vimalakirti Sutra translation, as it travels through China, Korea, Japan, and America. Thich Nhat Hanh's hammer striking the other hand shows how suffering is shared. Junka asks lay people, the receivers in the three wheels of giver, receiver, and gift, to share the teaching, citing a karate teacher's advice to do it "another thousand times." Compassion then gets its own turn: karuna is set apart from metta and pictured as a down feather whose quill stays sharp. Junka closes with the advice to keep the sharp end pointed at oneself.

So yesterday, I had to get this off my chest before I start the actual dharma talk.

I was a good little Zen person and I turned off all of my notifications on all of my devices—my watch, my phone—and then went to bed because I find sesshin to be extremely tiring and I wanted all the sleep I could get.
I woke up this morning to look at my phone only because it's also my alarm clock to see a picture of the nine-pound baby boy that my daughter-in-law had just given birth to.

And I want to thank you all for your well wishes of health to my daughter-in-law and my son and my grandson as they are recovering from giving birth and being born because they were in the well-being ceremony this morning.
So, okay, that's the big news.
Yay.
Pardon me.
Look a little bit more like that.
Is that good?
Okay, I'll try not to use any P's or S's if I put it that close to my mouth.
But so this is all so simple, isn't it?
In about 500 BCE, Buddha realized that no one is satisfied.
We all think, "I hate that, and I want that."
And if I only got rid of all I hate and I got everything that I wanted, it would be great.
But the Buddha realized that this was irrational.
He also realized that everything's changing; nothing stays the way we want it to be.
That everything is interconnected to the point that it is essentially one giant network.
This is profound, but basically simple.
He decided to teach this, and from all accounts, people ate it up, so much so that they wanted to remember it.
The only problem was that nobody could write yet, so they memorized it.
And problematically, the Buddha had a habit, in fact a teaching, of trying to teach his simple concepts to people at a level they understood.
So he explained his teachings in many different ways.
To keep track, people made lists as a mnemonic device.
They also made lists of things that other smart people that had heard and interpreted the Buddha's teachings said.
In his translation of the *Vimalakirti Sutra*, Robert Thurman attempted to make a list of all the lists and he came up with eighty-five lists.
And that was just from India.
The rest of us hadn't even gotten involved yet.
Thurman's list also includes lists that are lists of other lists, and it gets overwhelming.
And if when I first spoke, you were thinking he should have started with the lists of the four noble truths and the eightfold noble path, then congratulations.
You've proven to us how different sects arise.
So then writing happens.
Oops, my computer completely lost its place.
So then writing happens.
And when writing happens, it's in a culture of scarcity, where more and richer is synonymous with better.
So now we have six-legged white elephants, innumerable thrones of gold and jewels, and a hundred thousand million culprits.
The teachings are still so clear and so important that they continue to spread.
And one guy carries them over the mountains, the Himalayas for goodness sake.
And this is really not what my computer is supposed to be doing to me right now, sorry.
Technological stuff.
I usually do this on my iPad, but that wouldn't work here.
So we'll change it to this and this should make it happen less.
I apologize.
So and according to legend, this one guy carries the teachings across the mountains, the Himalayas, into China.
And here they run straight into the reductiveness of the Dao and the hierarchy of Confucius.
And people use the teachings for verbal combat of all things.
Of course, now we have writing.
So we have the game summaries of the combat, so that we have koans to contemplate.
And we have verses written about both the combat and interpretations of both the game summary and the verses.
And somebody wanders off with the teachings into the three kingdoms of Korea.
From there, the king of an area called Pakche literally presents them as a gift in exchange for military support to the rulers of a little part of an island off his eastern shore.
The rulers of that island kingdom, which is called Yamato, believe, as do many people of faith, that religious rights can buy you favors from the gods.
In Japanese, this is termed Genzai Ryaku, which is translated as "this world benefits."
In Latin, it might be termed *quid pro quo*.

They start promoting the rituals of this foreign religion in parallel with their own polytheistic animistic local faith, hoping that they can cover their bases with all the gods and protect their kingdom and more importantly, their rule over the kingdom.
The new faith is particularly attractive as it can be placed under state control and the monks regulated and used as tax collectors in addition to praying.
The ranks of monks are actually standardized to match those of state officials.

They like it so much that they spread the faith faster than the new monks can translate the now voluminous teachings of the Buddha and the thousand years of philosophers, scribes, commentators, and poets that follow the teachings of the Buddha.
They follow it in so they just start chanting things by reading the names of the characters out loud without translating them.
A significant hybridization with local beliefs changes both the teachings of Buddhism and the local religion, giving rise to Shinto as we now know it and forever changing Buddhism.
And Yamato grows and its borders, it grows its borders and it changes its name to Nihon, which in the West we mispronounce with a J as Japan.

In their spare time, the monks write more poems about the moon reflected in buckets of water, dew on blades of grass and mountains walking, and another monk writes a commentary on that poem and on and on.
And finally two different priests bring all of this Japanese tradition to the United States.
A Rinzai priest at the turn of the 1900s and a Soto priest in the middle of the 20th century.
The Soto priest arrives in the western town of San Francisco at a time when many Americans are craving something other than the faith of their fathers.
And they try to learn this new iteration of everything that has gone before, subtly changing it yet again.
As it runs into western psychological theories, acute societal changes and other Buddhism's that now meet because the dualistic world is now as interconnected as the Dharma world is said to be.
The faith is stripped of some of its more magical aspects as it is hybridized with scientific rationalism.
Westerners, typically of European origin and fairly affluent, with the fervor of converts practice as monks and lay clothing.
Some ordain but continue to lead full lives as lay people, an innovation that is rare in Asian countries.
New commentaries arise influenced by western needs and understandings.
And again troubled by the fact that the Dharma has now come down through at least seven different languages before English, 128 generations after the Buddha, and it is so complicated.
And yet all of it, all of it, is about greed, hate, delusion, suffering, impermanence and non-self.
In the midst of all of this complexity we can viscerally feel the truth of this.
I feel bad when I don't have what I want or when I'm forced to be with something I don't want.
I've lived long enough, I've lived long enough, I've lived long enough.
I've lived long enough and acquired enough things to know that material things and wealth don't stop the feeling of dissatisfaction.
I've watched too many friends and relatives die, too many perfect marriages dissolve, too many friendships end to think that things are permanent.
Non-self is tricky but also both intellectually and viscerally obvious, although it's a little bit uncomfortable to think about.
Our ego wants so, so much to be permanent and completely independent from anyone else.
But our boundaries are much more porous than that.
Leaving aside the fact that since we entered this room we've all inhaled little bits of each other.
I'm sorry but it's true.
Whether you like what I'm saying or not, I have changed the way you think.
And your facial expressions and reactions have changed the way I think.
Beyond that, we know we are all connected far more than the Western concept of self allows.
And sympathy and empathy are not just constructs within oneself.
Thich Nhat Hanh gave a famous Dharma talk in which he described working on a carpentry project.
He explained that because he was right-handed, sometimes his right hand in which he held the hammer accidentally hit his left hand in which he held the nail.
He pointed out that the left hand did not take the hammer and hit the right hand with it for revenge because both hands were part of the same whole and the hole felt the suffering of the left thumb.
This phenomenon happens even at a distance.

When a Palestinian father goes for food aid and returns to the school in Gaza where his family was sheltering, only to find it's been flattened by an Israeli bomb and his family is buried in the rubble.
We all feel that.
When the sister of the Israeli pilot who dropped the bomb was raped and killed in her home on a kibbutz by a Hamas terrorist, we all felt that.

Closer to home, we all felt the sense of panic and loss of the high school student in a farming community like the Skagit Valley that surrounds you when she returns home from classes to find that her father has been detained by ICE while working his job picking in the fields to give her a better life.
So what does that have to do with us?
Especially those of us who are lay people, the focus of this year's practice period.
If you feel the pull to be a cleric, to leave home and become a monastic, or to stay home in a lay life but put on the robes, please do.
If nothing else, you'll save a fortune on hair care products during your lifetime.

Everything I mentioned earlier—all the lists, the fantastical stories, the carrying to China, the sailing to Japan, coming to America, the poems, the commentaries, the explanations—are all because of clerics.
We need clerics to wrap and deliver the gift of the Buddhist teaching.
But there's another list in that eighty-five list list: the emptiness of the three wheels—giver, receiver, and gift.
The gift of the Buddhist teaching and the clerical giver are pointless without the receiver, and that's the lay people.
When you get this gift, I implore you not to leave it on your shelf neatly arranged in alphabetical order with your other gifts, only to be enjoyed privately.
As lay people, we are the interface between Buddhism and the rest of the world.
We don't have to dress differently.
We don't go door to door.
We don't hand out leaflets at the airport.
We just live the Dharma moment by moment in the world outside.
So take the gift out, listen to the instructions you were given with the gift, and share the hell out of it.
Because the gift of the teachings is universal.
Because the gift of the teachings is universal compassion.
Through universal compassion, we can help save all beings.

Now, I know that sounds trite, and I always think that when people bring it up in dharma talks, especially in the current political climate, how can our paltry efforts heal the world, especially when destructive forces hold power?
And much of our effort revolves around sitting on a cushion.
One of the teachers I've had longest in my life has no idea he teaches Zen; he's a staunch Catholic.
And Rokodan and Hyashiha Shtorokaratedo Salerno Sensei taught me that you can never chop down a tree with a single axe strike.
You just keep chipping away.
In class, one of his favorite pieces of advice is "another thousand times."
Just do it another thousand times.
So get off your cushion.
Leave the temple.
Go out in the world and start saving it.
Smile.
Give someone emotional support.
Greet your red cap wearing neighbor with kindness.
Stop buying detergent and plastic bottles.
Put solar panels on your house.
Charge your electric car with those solar panels.
Speak out.
Vote.
Call refugees.
Give money to or volunteer for good causes.
Just leave a bigger tip at the coffee shop.
And on and on, a thousand times, from tens of thousands of practitioners, over hundreds of thousands of days, and the mountains begin to move.
Now that would be an excellent place to end the talk.
But I had thought about a thought about compassion that I need to share.
At the conclusion of the sesshin that opened practice period, I was chatting with Nomon Tin after Raizelah's ordination, and the topic of compassion came up.
I had just given my way seeking mind talk the day before, and for those of you who heard that talk, my apologies.
But you may remember that my failure at marriage was a big catalyst for me becoming a Buddhist.

During that period of my life, Nomon had suffered through quite a few dokusan sessions that covered the mess that was my relationship, and he commented that he had been struck by the way I had spoken kindly of my ex during my talk.
I replied that age gives you the perspective and that sometimes you realize that the other person isn't the only asshole in your story.
He commented that he had meant to say that I had been compassionate, but maybe that was the Ken Oats version of being compassionate.
In fact, I was being compassionate, but being compassionate to her involved admitting to myself that I was part of the problem.
This brings up a point about compassion.
Sometimes we conflate compassion with love or kindness, but there's a reason that there are different words for those concepts.
Love is warm and soft and fuzzy, and so is kindness.
I could ignite a bomb of love or kindness in this room and nobody would get hurt.
Compassion is from the Latin word *compati*, which literally means to suffer with.
This word was chosen to translate the Pali word *karuna*, which is described as the desire to remove harm and suffering from others.
Even in Pali, it's distinct from *meta*, which is the desire to bring about well-being and happiness, and is generally translated in English as loving kindness.
This distinction appears in our precept ceremony as well, as we vow separately to refrain from harmful conduct, which is *karuna*, and to cultivate beneficial conduct, which is *meta*.
Both of these are distinctly different from the concept of pity or to feel sorry for someone.
Compassion is like those little down feathers inside the coats and vests we all like so much in the Pacific Northwest.
Down can be soft, but there's a sharp end to the quill that can be irritating, and sometimes it can be very, very painful.
Compassion has sharp edges and points hidden inside the warm fuzzies.
Love and kindness would catch somebody who is falling down to protect them from pain.
Compassion sometimes lets them fall so they learn not to stumble in the future.
Catching them would be *meta*, but letting them fall might be *karuna*.

Love and kindness intervene to stop self-destructive behavior, while sometimes compassion just watches to prevent serious injury, while letting the person hit rock bottom and figure out for themselves that they need to get help.
Sometimes being compassionate irritates or cuts the ego that thinks you're separate, that somehow you are being good to someone else as if you were separate.
Sometimes the sharp bit cuts the person to whom you're extending compassion.
Sometimes the sharp bit cuts the person to whom you're extending compassion.
The hurt can be necessary in either case.
So while being compassionate, be aware that it isn't always easy.
You might get hurt, suffer, or realize uncomfortable truths about yourself.
More importantly, be aware that in extending compassion to others, you might inflict pain on them or allow them to suffer temporarily.
Try to be skillful.
Try to use the soft end of the feather and keep the sharp end pointed at yourself.
But you might inadvertently use the sharp end, and in some cases, the sharp end might be what's necessary.
I want to thank you for listening to my ramblings today and during the rest of practice period for those of you who are willing to suffer enough that you signed up for my class.
And I hope I have not led you astray.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Things are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to win them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become.*
